---
title: "CLT Convergence for Normal Samples"
format: html
editor: visual
---

## Background

The distributions being averaged here are normal distributions. This distribution is characterized by following roughly a standard bell curve, with the most common result being at the mean and results further from the mean being progressively less common. Because this is the distribution that I am testing the means for, it will probably take a pretty low n in order to approach normality.

## Data

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# Monte Carlo Simulation: Baseline Control (Standard Normal Parent)
# ==============================================================================

library(ggplot2)

# 1. Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6418)

# 2. Simulation parameters
B <- 10000                            # Number of Monte Carlo repetitions
n_values <- c(2, 5, 10, 30, 100)      # Sample sizes to test

# 3. Initialize results data frame
results <- data.frame()

# 4. Run Monte Carlo loop for Standard Normal N(0, 1)
for (n in n_values) {
  
  # Draw B sample means from Standard Normal N(0, 1)
  sample_means <- replicate(B, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))
  
  # A. Calculate Q-Q Plot R-squared
  theo_quantiles <- qnorm(ppoints(B))
  sample_quantiles <- sort(sample_means)
  r2_val <- cor(theo_quantiles, sample_quantiles)^2
  
  # B. Calculate Sample Skewness (3rd standardized moment)
  m3 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^3)
  s3 <- sd(sample_means)^3
  skew_val <- abs(m3 / s3)
  
  # C. Calculate Excess Kurtosis (4th standardized moment - 3)
  m4 <- mean((sample_means - mean(sample_means))^4)
  s4 <- sd(sample_means)^4
  kurt_val <- abs((m4 / s4) - 3)
  
  # Append to results
  results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
    n = n,
    R2 = r2_val,
    Skewness = skew_val,
    Excess_Kurtosis = kurt_val
  ))
}

# ==============================================================================
# Generate Plots with 3xSE Threshold Overlays
# ==============================================================================

# Graph 1: Q-Q Plot R^2 vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.98)
p1 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = R2)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.98, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.98, label = "Threshold (0.98)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("1. Quantile Alignment (" * R^2 * " vs. Sample Size)")),
    subtitle = expression("Standard Normal Parent (" * B == 10000 * ")"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = expression("Q-Q Plot " * R^2)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.975, 1.001)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph 2: Skewness vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.075)
p2 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Skewness)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "darkorange", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.075, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.075, label = "Threshold (0.075)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "2. Asymmetry (Skewness vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Standard Normal Parent (" * B == 10000 * ")"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Skewness"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.1)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Graph 3: Excess Kurtosis vs. Sample Size (Threshold = 0.15)
p3 <- ggplot(results, aes(x = n, y = Excess_Kurtosis)) +
  geom_line(color = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "forestgreen", size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.15, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_values), y = 0.15, label = "Threshold (0.15)", 
           vjust = -0.5, hjust = 1, color = "firebrick", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "3. Tail Weight (Excess Kurtosis vs. Sample Size)",
    subtitle = expression("Standard Normal Parent (" * B == 10000 * ")"),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Excess Kurtosis"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_values) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.2)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display plots
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(p3)

# Graph A: Histogram (Multimodality Check)
df_n2 <- data.frame(sample_means = results[["2"]])
v1 <- ggplot(df_n2, aes(x = sample_means)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
    bins = 50, 
    fill = "steelblue", 
    color = "white", 
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_density(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("Visual Check for Unimodality")),
    subtitle = expression("Using n = 2, the lowest n that passed all tests"),
    x = "Sample Mean",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  
# Graph B: Normal Q-Q Plot for n = 2
v2 <- ggplot(df_n2, aes(sample = sample_means)) +
  stat_qq(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = expression(bold("Normal Q-Q Plot (n = 2)")),
    subtitle = "Exposes Severe Right-Skewness (C-Shaped Curvature)",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# Display plots
print(v1)
print(v2)
 
```

## Conclusion

The means of normal distributions pass all tests immediately, even at n=2. While initially a worrying conclusion, this actually makes a lot of sense. If I were to take this conclusion and run it to its logical extreme , running the simulation with n=1, this would functionally be no different than creating one single binomial with 10,000 samples. Of course that's going to look like a normal distribution.

## $$\boxed{n=\text{1}}$$
